title: Independent ideas. Extraordinary finds.
intro: A daily selection of independent games and useful Android apps, with original F7 insights and links to their creators.

entries.name: KubeFactory
entries.summary: KubeFactory turns a live Kubernetes cluster into a first-person factory floor. Nodes become platforms and pods become machines you walk up to, each carrying a type plate with its real pod name, an icon for the workload and a screen with dashboard, metrics, logs and storage views. Connecting needs only a kubeconfig, so the machines you inspect are the ones actually running, and a browser sandbox with four demo worlds lets you learn the controls before touching a real cluster.
features: Nodes are walkable platforms and pods are machines labelled with their real pod names
Machine screens switch between dashboard, metrics, logs and storage views
Connects with a kubeconfig directly, with no kubectl installation required
A datapad collects logs, events and an audit ledger while tools need hold-to-confirm actions
Foreman answers plain-language questions with checked proposals that still need your approval
Four sandbox demo worlds model a web shop, a home-media stack, Home Assistant and a build farm
entries.insight: Operations dashboards flatten everything to the same size of rectangle. KubeFactory restores scale: a crash-looping pod is a machine that pulses on your minimap, so the failing part of the system becomes somewhere you can walk to instead of a row you scroll past.

entries.name: TopHat-ShooterOS
entries.summary: TopHat-ShooterOS is a bullet-heaven in Nim and Raylib where the whole game is presented as a desktop operating system. You are one process defending the TOPHAT kernel, so the start menu runs WAVE0.exe, cosmetics come from CHROMA.db, the manual opens in a terminal and MODS.exe changes the rules. Behind the interface sit 88 power-ups, 28 enemy types, 21 bosses and five modes, including online play for up to 16 people.
features: Menus, shop, manual and mod manager are presented as desktop applications
Five modes: a 60-wave campaign, the Deep Recovery roguelite, 20-minute Time Survival, online PvP for 2-16 players and a sandbox
88 power-ups, 28 enemy types and 21 bosses split into separate mode rosters
Elemental build families with auras, orbs, walls, turrets, a dash and a rerollable level-up draft
Modding through Lua, with MODS.exe exposed inside the game shell
Sound and music are generated on first launch, so no asset files ship with the build
entries.insight: The operating-system conceit is not decoration: making the shop, manual and mod loader into windows changes how a run-and-gun is learned. Players browse the rules the way they would any app, which is why a dense 88-power-up roster stays approachable.

entries.name: Microcosm
entries.summary: Microcosm is a compact 4X strategy game written in Python on top of the Pyxel retro engine, with online play and a rule reference built into the game rather than bolted on. The author ships standalone builds for macOS, Linux and Windows, publishes the package on PyPI as microcosm-4x, and documents a local game server you can run yourself for people who would rather host than join.
features: A 4X strategy game built as a Python project on the Pyxel pixel engine
Global multiplayer, with the developer documenting UPnP as the network requirement
Self-hostable local game server started with a single Python command
Standalone builds for macOS on ARM64, Linux on x86 and Windows
Installable as the microcosm-4x package from PyPI for anyone already running Python 3.12+
A rules wiki maintained both in-game and on the project's GitHub wiki
entries.insight: Microcosm is interesting as a small-team answer to a genre that usually needs hundreds of person-hours: the retro engine keeps the surface tiny, and the hosting model is the same idea you would meet in a self-hosted feed reader rather than in a strategy game.

entries.name: Bansoko

price.label: Free on itch.io and GitHub Releases

entries.summary: Bansoko is a space-themed reworking of Soko-Ban, the 1984 MS-DOS puzzle, rebuilt in Python with the Pyxel engine. You are a scavenger directing a remote-controlled robot through abandoned ships, pushing cargo into bays with a rule the game states plainly: crates can be pushed, never pulled. Unlimited undo is part of the design, which turns a puzzle famous for irreversible mistakes into one you can argue with.
features: Reimagines the 1984 Soko-Ban crate-pushing puzzle as deep-space salvage
Push-only cargo rule carried over from the original design
Undo as many steps as needed, so a blocked layout can always be talked back
Standalone Windows and Linux builds bundle Python and every library used
Also installable as the bansoko package with pip on Python 3.11+
Distributed through the developer's itch.io page and GitHub Releases
entries.insight: Undo is the whole editorial argument here. Soko-Ban's 1984 difficulty came partly from puzzles that punished a single wrong push; shipping a remake that removes that punishment while keeping the push-only rule is a deliberate design position, not a convenience.

entries.name: Slide Puzzle
entries.summary: Slide Puzzle is a straightforward take on the sliding-tile picture puzzle, built in Godot and published as a complete open-source project with prebuilt desktop archives. Its interest is in the small set of knobs the developer chose to expose: the board size is configurable, any image can become the puzzle, tile numbers can be shown or hidden, and both mouse and keyboard input are supported.
features: Configurable board size, so the same puzzle can be 3x3 or far larger
Custom background images turn any picture into the tile layout
Tile numbers can be shown or hidden for players who want a numeric or a visual puzzle
Both mouse and keyboard input are supported
Prebuilt Windows x64 and Linux archives published on GitHub Releases
Godot project published under an MIT license
entries.insight: There is a lesson in keeping a one-mechanic game open source: the four options the author exposes, board size, image, numbering and input, are exactly the ones that decide whether a familiar puzzle is still yours.

entries.name: cTetris
entries.summary: cTetris is a deliberately minimal implementation of Tetris in C using Raylib, published with the rules written out rather than left implicit. The readme documents a 20x10 grid, level-driven drop speed, wall and floor kicks, a half-second lock timer, a 15-move budget that forces a hard drop, and a high score persisted to disk, which makes the project useful as a readable reference for how modern falling-block games actually resolve a piece.
features: 20x10 grid with level-scaled drop speed in plain C on top of Raylib
Rotation with wall and floor kicks, soft drop and hard drop
0.5-second lock timer that resets on movement, with an airborne and grounded distinction
A 15-move budget per piece that forces a hard drop when exhausted
High score kept on disk between sessions
Keyboard controls with pause, restart, mute and a light/dark theme toggle
entries.insight: Most open-source Tetris clones stop at the grid. cTetris documents the parts that decide competitive feel, lock timers, move budgets, kick behaviour, which is why it reads less like a toy and more like a specification you could argue with.

entries.name: Bim!
entries.summary: Bim! is an open-source online multiplayer game for Android in the last-man-standing mould: up to four players share a small arena, dropping bombs to break crates, expose bonuses and finish off opponents. Its distinguishing idea is the feature draft. As you play you unlock gameplay modifiers, and each match combines your selection with your opponents', so a round can change shape without anyone buying an advantage.
features: Up to four players per online match in a bomb-and-crates arena
Breaking crates can reveal bonuses such as extra bombs or longer blast radius
Unlockable gameplay features are selected before a match and combine with opponents' choices
The developer states that every selected feature affects all players equally, with no pay to win
Published in beta on Google Play, with APK releases, F-Droid and Obtainium as alternatives
Code is AGPL-3.0 and most graphics and sounds are CC BY-SA 4.0, credited per file
entries.insight: Letting players draft modifiers is the rare mobile design that trades balance for conversation: matches become readable as a clash of chosen rules rather than of accounts, and the licence list behind it shows how much non-code work a small game carries.

entries.name: SparkleDNS
entries.summary: SparkleDNS is a lightweight DNS-over-HTTPS client for Android that runs a local VPN holding nothing but DNS. Queries go to the resolver you choose over RFC 8484 while all other traffic keeps using your normal connection, and the activity views, blocklists and logs stay on the device. It ships without analytics or Google Play Services and documents a signing fingerprint so you can verify an APK before installing.
features: Local VPN that captures only DNS traffic and forwards it to a chosen DoH server
One-tap connect and disconnect, including a Quick Settings tile
Server switching that restarts the tunnel automatically, with a built-in latency and protocol test
24-hour and 7-day activity charts, a filterable live log and one-tap blocking, computed on device
Per-app DNS so selected apps bypass the tunnel
Custom blocklists by URL, including HaGeZi presets refreshed daily or weekly
entries.insight: Splitting DNS from the rest of the tunnel is the interesting engineering choice: a VPN API is used only for packet selection, which keeps a privacy tool from becoming the bottleneck for everything else on the phone.

entries.name: AlarmClockXtreme
entries.summary: AlarmClockXtreme is an open-source Android alarm clock aimed at heavy sleepers and shift workers. It uses Android's exact alarm path, restores schedules after a reboot and keeps a Direct Boot fallback for the next alarm, then backs the wake-up with thirty dismiss challenge types and shift patterns such as 4-on-4-off, Panama and Pitman. Releases are signed APKs published with checksums and certificate fingerprints.
features: Exact alarm scheduling with recovery after reboot and a minimal Direct Boot fallback
Thirty dismiss challenge types, from math and typing to walking, NFC, barcode and photo match, chainable into missions
Rotating shift support for DDNNO, 4-on-4-off, Panama, DuPont and Pitman cycles, with vacation and holiday skips
Alarms can play a ringtone, an HTTPS radio stream, Spotify or saved sounds, with light fade-up via Philips Hue or DIRIGERA
Webhooks and Tasker broadcasts fire on alarm events, and a wake-readiness check warns before bedtime
Today tab adds local weather, air quality and sunrise timing alongside timers, world clocks and Wear OS controls
entries.insight: The interesting engineering is unglamorous: exact alarms, reboot restoration, Direct Boot fallback and published checksums. Those are the parts that decide whether a clock app deserves to be trusted with a 4am shift, rather than whether it looks nice.

entries.name: CarpeLines
entries.summary: CarpeLines displays live, word-by-word lyrics for whatever is playing on your phone, without owning a music library. It attaches to the active Android media session, resolves lyrics from seven sources including embedded tags, sibling .lrc files and several streaming providers, and renders them with word-level timing, character-level handling for CJK text and translations or romanization kept in sync.
features: Word-level highlighting, with character-by-character animation and a spring effect for Chinese, Japanese and Korean lyrics
Reads the system media session through NotificationListenerService and MediaSessionManager, so it drives the player you already use
Seven lyric sources: embedded tags, sibling .lrc files, QQ Music, NetEase Cloud Music, Kugou, LRCLIB and Apple Music, in a configurable order
Duet and backing-vocal layouts with separate columns and per-line styling
Three widgets, including a now-playing bar, a lyric control card and a square tile
Full-screen page samples the current album artwork for its palette, with fluid and album-blur animated backgrounds
entries.insight: CarpeLines is built around an absence: no audio engine and no library of its own. Handing playback back to the active session is what lets one overlay serve every player on the device, which is the opposite of the usual all-in-one music app.

entries.name: Grove
entries.summary: Grove tracks streaks as a forest. Each habit you plant becomes a procedurally generated fractal tree that grows through real stages as days pass, and the app offers two modes: abstinence, which records relapses with notes, and check-in, which builds streaks while letting you excuse days or freeze a streak. Everything runs offline, with widgets, milestone reminders and biometric or PIN locking for privacy.
features: Each habit is a unique procedurally generated fractal tree that advances through growth stages
Abstinence mode tracks current streak, all-time best and every relapse with notes
Check-in mode supports excused days and streak freezes so planned breaks do not reset progress
Four layouts: 3D vertical drum, horizontal carousel, compact grid and list
Live tree and calendar home-screen widgets plus milestone reminders
Biometric, fingerprint or PIN locking, local backups and 14 languages, all offline
entries.insight: Streak apps usually show a number and a calendar grid. Grove's growth model changes what a lapse means visually, and its two modes admit that quitting something and starting something need different record-keeping even when the interface looks the same.

entries.name: Moke
entries.summary: Moke is a native Android SSH and mosh terminal with a userspace Tailscale client built in, so a tailnet can be reached without taking over the system VPN slot. It handles password, PEM-key and Tailscale SSH authentication, per-host proxies, multiple background sessions with remote tmux management, and SFTP transfers that resume. Network credentials and tailnet login state are stored through the Android Keystore.
features: SSH and mosh with password, PEM private-key and Tailscale SSH identity authentication
Built-in userspace Tailscale for official or self-hosted control servers, leaving the system VPN slot free
HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS4 and SOCKS5 proxies selectable per host
Multiple background sessions, remote tmux management and port forwarding bound to the device loopback only
SFTP browsing with resumable uploads and downloads
Terminal with custom extra keys, IME and text-block input, fonts and colour schemes, in English or Chinese
entries.insight: Shipping a userspace tailnet client inside a terminal is the pragmatic call: it gives a phone direct reach to machines that only exist on a private network, without asking the user to run a second always-on VPN app.

entries.name: Usugami
entries.summary: Usugami is an offline PDF toolkit for Android that converts photos, ID cards, Word, PowerPoint, Excel and EPUB files into PDFs and then works on them: read, annotate, print, split, merge, reorganise, rotate, crop, number, watermark, sign, compress, flatten and redact. It was called PDFer before version 1.2.0, and the app itself carries no internet permission, so nothing is uploaded.
features: Converts images, Word, PowerPoint, Excel and EPUB documents into PDFs on the device
Full editing set: split, merge, reorganise, rotate, crop, page numbering, watermark, sign, compress, flatten and redact
Three signed editions: the main app, a smaller Lite build with no Google code, and an OCR build with PaddleOCR models bundled inside
OCR editions either use Play services recognition or run entirely offline, depending on which you install
Long-press app shortcuts jump straight to Scan document, Images to PDF and Merge PDF
No ads, no tracking, no account and no uploads, distributed as APKs with Obtainium updates
entries.insight: Splitting one app into three signed editions is an honest answer to a hard constraint: on-device recognition needs a model, so the author lets you choose between a small APK, no Google code at all, or a bigger file that works with no network ever.

entries.name: Repertoire
entries.summary: Repertoire organises the work of performing rather than the work of note-taking. Each piece in your library keeps its PDF sheet music viewable in-app, Markdown notes for annotations and lyrics, reference images, audio files you can slow down or shift in pitch, and video links, while practice sessions are logged per piece so you can see what you last worked on and how often.
features: Pieces stored with title, composer or artist and custom tags in list or grid views
In-app PDF sheet music, Markdown notes, images, audio with speed and pitch control, and video links
Practice session logs showing when a piece was last played and how many sessions it has
Search and filter by title, composer, tags, genre, difficulty and practice history
Whole-library backup and restore
Android via F-Droid or GitHub APK, Windows and Linux builds, plus a live web version
entries.insight: Musicians already have notes apps; what they rarely have is audio that changes speed and pitch without leaving the piece it belongs to. Making practice history a first-class field turns a filing cabinet into something closer to a rehearsal log.
